article_title: Towards an Evidence Framework for Emerging Educational Technologies
citation: Roschelle, J., Ruiz, P., Means, B., Griffiths, R., Lee, K. (2026 April). Towards an Evidence Framework for Emerging Educational Technologies. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/289
title: The Rhizome: evidence as an interactive conversation rather than a seal of approval
description: The Rhizome is a workshop-generated visualization of evidence in which evidence is 'an interactive, informative conversation rather than a simple seal of approval'. It treats evidence as seldom unitary, with 'aspects that are more central and well-supported and aspects that are more thinly developed or in need of further investigation', and frames evidence use as a multi-step process spanning acceptability, adoption, implementation planning, and continuous improvement.
requirements: Requires a complementary scheme clarifying study-type purposes, design quality factors, measures, and the degree to which evidence supports claims
constraints: The article states it would likely fall short as an organizing metaphor for evidence production, and that over-use could weaken evidentiary standards
target_learning_goals: Evidence-based edtech adoption and continuous improvement decisions
examples: One workshop leader imagined an evidence chatbot replacing an evidence report and allowing for interrogation over time
key_sources: Roschelle, J., Ruiz, P., Means, B., Griffiths, R., Lee, K. (2026 April). Towards an Evidence Framework for Emerging Educational Technologies. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/289

article_title: Purpose Before Policy: Academic Integrity, Generative AI, and Rhetorical Stance
citation: Tristan B. Taylor & Travis LaCroix. (2026). Purpose before policy: academic integrity, generative AI, and rhetorical stance. Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-026-01706-1
title: Rhetorical framework for institutional identity: Burke's terministic screen, Bitzer's rhetorical situation, and Booth's rhetorical stance and its three corruptions
description: The article assembles three rhetorical frameworks to analyse how universities construct institutional identity through mission statements. Burke supplies a philosophical account of meaning-making as symbolic action, centred on the terministic screen, where every linguistic choice simultaneously "reflects, selects, and deflects reality". Bitzer delineates the conditions under which rhetorical action is intelligible and effective, defining the rhetorical situation as exigence plus constraints. Booth identifies the characteristic modes of rhetorical failure: the Entertainer's stance (ethos over substance), the Advertiser's stance (pathos at the cost of accuracy), and the Pedant's stance. The article applies these to mission statements from the U15, Russell Group, and Ivy League as a diagnostic lens on aspirational institutional discourse.
requirements: Application requires publicly available mission statements as the genre of institutional discourse analysed, articulating official self-understanding to heterogeneous audiences
constraints: The authors state the analysis is illustrative rather than exhaustive and not representative in a statistical sense; it is a diagnostic lens on aspirational discourse, not evidence of day-to-day institutional practice
target_learning_goals: interpreting institutional policy discourse around emerging technologies
examples: The article reads the University of Waterloo's motto-based mission as the Entertainer's stance and Dartmouth's 'most promising students ... responsible leadership' as the Advertiser's stance.
key_sources: Tristan B. Taylor & Travis LaCroix. (2026). Purpose before policy: academic integrity, generative AI, and rhetorical stance. Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-026-01706-1

article_title: Preschool musicality is associated with school-age communication abilities through genes related to rhythmicity
citation: Lucía de Hoyos, Ellen Verhoef, Aysu Okbay, Janne R. Vermeulen, Celeste Figaroa, Miriam Lense, Simon E. Fisher, Reyna L. Gordon & Beate St Pourcain. (2025). Preschool musicality is associated with school-age communication abilities through genes related to rhythmicity. npj Science of Learning 10:39. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00329-y
title: MAPLE framework and Atypical Rhythm Risk Hypothesis as accounts of musicality-language links
description: The article situates its findings within two theoretical frameworks: the Musical Abilities, Pleiotropy, Language, and Environment (MAPLE) framework, "which states that musicality and language share genetic variation and therefore musicality and language are interrelated", and the Atypical Rhythm Risk Hypothesis, "which proposes that rhythm impairment is associated with delays in speech/language abilities". The study's genetic results — shared rhythmicity effects on speech-related communication — are interpreted as consistent with both accounts.
requirements: Genetic instruments (polygenic scores) for rhythmicity and longitudinal phenotypes ordered in developmental time to test directionality
constraints: PGS analyses account for only a small proportion of phenotypic variance (incremental R2: 0.004–0.01)
requires replication in an independent population-based cohort
target_learners: typically developing children from infancy through adolescence
examples: The mediation-style SEM in ALSPAC showing PGS-rhythmicity-shared effects on school-age speech-related communication was read as consistent with these frameworks
key_sources: Lucía de Hoyos, Ellen Verhoef, Aysu Okbay, Janne R. Vermeulen, Celeste Figaroa, Miriam Lense, Simon E. Fisher, Reyna L. Gordon & Beate St Pourcain. (2025). Preschool musicality is associated with school-age communication abilities through genes related to rhythmicity. npj Science of Learning 10:39. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00329-y

article_title: Social interaction shapes and boosts second language learning: virtual reality can show us how
citation: Ana Zappa, Mel Slater & Antoni Rodriguez-Fornells. (2025). Social interaction shapes and boosts second language learning: virtual reality can show us how. npj Science of Learning 10:90. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00381-8
title: Proposed extension of the Revised Hierarchical Model: socially enriched contexts foster more direct L2 word-to-concept links from the start of learning
description: The article builds on the Revised Hierarchical Model, in which "the L2 lexicon initially relies on L1 translations during early learning and later develops direct connections to conceptual meanings as proficiency increases". The authors propose an extension in which socially enriched, multimodal and interactive contexts facilitate "more direct links between L2 lexical items and conceptual representations compared to learning in classical non-social settings", allowing learners to bypass reliance on L1 translations from the beginning. The extension explicitly incorporates the four factors of multimodality, embodiment, interaction and social feedback, and is offered as an empirically testable target for VR-based research.
requirements: Testing requires paradigms that manipulate social-enrichment factors while controlling linguistic input, e.g., via VR with virtual agents whose gaze, gestures and object interaction can be varied.
constraints: The extension is a proposal; the article states it should be empirically tested using VR to compare word learning outcomes across socially enriched and traditional contexts, and presents it as a model to refine rather than a validated result.
target_learning_goals: Direct mapping of L2 word forms to conceptual meaning; vocabulary integration into the L2 lexicon
examples: The review's Fig. 2B depicts the extension, with stronger links between L2 wordforms and concepts under multimodal, social learning settings compared with classical non-social settings.
key_sources: Ana Zappa, Mel Slater & Antoni Rodriguez-Fornells. (2025). Social interaction shapes and boosts second language learning: virtual reality can show us how. npj Science of Learning 10:90. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00381-8

article_title: Rhythm for Reading: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Dr Ben Styles, Rebecca Clarkson, Katherine Fowler. (2014). Rhythm for Reading: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. http://www.controlled-trials.com/ISRCTN10404460/
title: Rhythm for Reading programme: weekly ten-minute rhythm-based exercises with musical notation for struggling readers
description: Rhythm for Reading is a ten-week course of weekly ten-minute sessions in which children take part in "rhythm-based exercises such as stamping, clapping and chanting, while reading musical notation". Up to ten children are taken out of lessons, sit in a semi-circle before an interactive whiteboard displaying musical notation, and chant and stamp along to pre-recorded audio files downloaded from the programme website. In this trial it was delivered to Year 7 pupils who had not reached a secure Level 4 in English at the end of Key Stage 2.
requirements: Sessions require a room with an interactive whiteboard or projector screen and access to the online audio and notation resources
constraints: The report states the mechanism by which Rhythm for Reading works is not well understood
Delivery was variable across schools owing to timetable constraints, with one school delivering only nine sessions to groups of 15-20 pupils
target_learners: Year 7 pupils who had not reached a secure Level 4 in English and/or reading at the end of Key Stage 2
target_learning_goals: reading ability, including sentence completion and passage comprehension
examples: In the EEF trial the developer delivered all sessions weekly between April and July 2013, and teaching assistants were trained to deliver the sessions to the waitlist control group in Year 8
key_sources: Dr Ben Styles, Rebecca Clarkson, Katherine Fowler. (2014). Rhythm for Reading: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. http://www.controlled-trials.com/ISRCTN10404460/

article_title: The Effects of a Music and Movement Program on Gait, Balance and Psychological Parametres of Adults with Cerebral Palsy
citation: Vasiliki Efraimidou, Maria Sidiropoulou, Paraskevi Giagazoglou, Miltiadis Proios, Vasileios Tsimaras, Anastasios Orologas. (2016). THE EFFECTS OF A MUSIC AND MOVEMENT PROGRAM ON GAIT, BALANCE AND PSYCHOLOGICAL PARAMETRES OF ADULTS WITH CEREBRAL PALSY. International Journal of Special Education, 31(2).
title: Make rhythm the center of movement interventions for people with cerebral palsy rather than background music
description: The article recommends that "clinicians should actively incorporate rhythmic music into movement intervention programs for people with CP because rhythmic music can be a powerful enhancer of the program", and that they should put "more emphasis into making rhythm as the center of the intervention rather than the background". Unlike preceding studies that used music only as background, this study made music the major intervening variable and reported significant improvements.
requirements: A structured program with music tracks of controlled meter and tempo (4/4, 70-90 bpm) synchronized to movement tasks
constraints: The study could not separate the differential effects of movement, psychological support and stimulating music
target_learners: athletes in throwing events with CP
target_learning_goals: improved gait, balance and psychological parameters
examples: The 8-week program paired walking, stretching and balance tasks with metronome-paced 4/4 music, with singing to open and close sessions
key_sources: Vasiliki Efraimidou, Maria Sidiropoulou, Paraskevi Giagazoglou, Miltiadis Proios, Vasileios Tsimaras, Anastasios Orologas. (2016). THE EFFECTS OF A MUSIC AND MOVEMENT PROGRAM ON GAIT, BALANCE AND PSYCHOLOGICAL PARAMETRES OF ADULTS WITH CEREBRAL PALSY. International Journal of Special Education, 31(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1111110

article_title: Rhinoplasty Education During Residency: Discussion of Current Barriers, Challenges, and Opportunities for Improvement.
citation: Khetpal Sumun, Hall Anne E., Ibrahim Yasmine, Nabili Vishad, Delong Michael R., Roostaeian Jason. (2026). Rhinoplasty Education During Residency: Discussion of Current Barriers, Challenges, and Opportunities for Improvement. Aesthetic Plastic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00266-025-05539-8
title: Barriers to learning rhinoplasty during residency include access, aesthetic judgment, surgical approach, tactile feedback reliance, faculty perception, and the practice model.
description: The review proposes a framework of barriers that obstruct rhinoplasty exposure and education during residency, summarized as: access (institutional factors including availability of cosmetic faculty and case volume), aesthetic judgment (synthesis of preoperative nasal anatomy with surgical maneuvers), approach (open, closed, or hybrid techniques affecting visualization and learning), touch (reliance on tactile feedback for maneuvers such as subperichondrial and subperiosteal plane dissection), perception (variable faculty and program leadership opinions on rhinoplasty's importance), and practice model (limited graduated autonomy compared to bilateral procedures). The authors state "these barriers may ultimately impact how trainees approach their clinical practice and their inclusion (or lack thereof) of rhinoplasty." This framework organizes the review's discussion of why rhinoplasty education is heterogeneous across programs.
requirements: Programs must recognize institutional factors including cosmetic faculty availability, case volume, and attending practice scope to address barriers.
constraints: The framework is derived from the authors' synthesis of the literature and their own clinical experience rather than from direct empirical testing of the barrier categories.
key_sources: Khetpal Sumun, Hall Anne E., Ibrahim Yasmine, Nabili Vishad, Delong Michael R., Roostaeian Jason. (2026). Rhinoplasty Education During Residency: Discussion of Current Barriers, Challenges, and Opportunities for Improvement. Aesthetic Plastic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00266-025-05539-8
